fact: Loveland's development code, as amended in March 2026, counts artificial turf as functional where it is regularly used for civic, community or recreational purposes, naming a playground, a sports field, a dog park or warm-up area of a park, and the playing area of a golf course or driving range.
quote: Functional Artificial Turfgrass means artificial turfgrass that is used for a functional purpose. This means it is located in a recreational use area or other space that is regularly used for civic, community, or recreational purposes, which may include a playground, sports field, a portion of a park (e.g., dog park area, warm-up area), and the playing area of a golf course or driving range.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Functional Artificial Turfgrass" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland’s three-entry prohibited plant list (noxious or invasive plants named by the United States or Colorado; nonfunctional turfgrass and nonfunctional artificial turfgrass on commercial, industrial, institutional and common interest community property, street rights-of-way, parkways, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors; and plants on a list the Director keeps) bars those plants from the city and has them removed during development or redevelopment.
quote: Prohibited Plant List. The following plants are not allowed in the City, and shall be removed during development or redevelopment if they are present on the subject property: … Plants that are identified as noxious, invasive, or prohibited in Loveland by the United States or the State of Colorado; … Nonfunctional turfgrass and/or nonfunctional artificial turfgrass on commercial, industrial, institutional, common interest community property, street right-of-way, parkways, parking lots, medians, or transportation corridors; and … Plants that are identified on the City’s list of prohibited plants, which is maintained by the Director.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.08.02.01.C, Prohibited Plant List (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view, Sec. 18.08.02.01.C; the section history shows only Ord. 6819 (effective 2026-03-17), so whether entry 2 is new or reworded is not shown on the page.

fact: Loveland's development code calls artificial turf nonfunctional when it serves no active purpose, including turf not regularly used for civic, community or recreational purposes or installed only for looks or low maintenance.
quote: Nonfunctional Artificial Turfgrass means artificial turfgrass that is not serving an active purpose. It includes artificial turfgrass that is not regularly used for civic, community, or recreational purposes, or that is installed only for aesthetic or maintenance purposes.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Nonfunctional Artificial Turfgrass" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's parking lot standards require the living groundcover in landscape separators to be water-wise landscape material rather than nonfunctional turfgrass.
quote: The living groundcover for landscape separators shall be water-wise landscape material (not nonfunctional turfgrass) and shall comply with subsection B.1, above.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.08.04.03, Parking Lots (as amended by Ord. 6819)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). Separators apply to large surface parking lots; the prohibited list (18.08.02.01.C) separately covers nonfunctional artificial turfgrass in parking lots.

fact: Loveland's development code defines an outdoor kennel as a facility where four or more household pets of the same species are temporarily housed, groomed, bred, boarded or trained, with an outdoor component such as dog runs.
quote: Kennel (Outdoor) means a facility in which four or more household pets of the same species are temporarily housed, groomed, bred, boarded, or trained, and may also be incidentally treated for medical conditions. The facility includes an outdoor component, such as dog runs.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Kennel (Outdoor)" (effective Nov. 20, 2018)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland lets a temporary accessory structure sit in a utility easement only if it won't alter or block drainage and the owner has the easement holder's written permission, and otherwise keeps accessory structures out of easements.
quote: The structure may be located within a utility easement provided: … The location of the structure will not alter or block drainage unless the structure is part of an approved stormwater management system. … The property owner obtains written permission from the easement holder. … Encroachments. Except as set forth in Section D above, accessory structures shall not encroach upon an easement, right-of-way, or a required sight triangle at a street intersection.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.04.07.02.D.1 and H, Accessory Structures (effective Jan. 20, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). D.1 sits under Temporary Accessory Structures.

fact: Loveland's code prohibits nonfunctional turfgrass and nonfunctional artificial turfgrass in the common landscape areas of single-family, duplex, townhome and multiplex developments, and asks commercial, industrial, institutional and common interest community landscape plans to mark each functional turf area and its use.
quote: Turfgrass Areas . All landscape plans for commercial, industrial, institutional, and common interest community property areas should delineate functional turfgrass areas and identify the associated functional use(s) of that turfgrass area. … Common landscape areas are those areas of land within a subject property that are either owned by a property owners' association or dedicated to the City or another governmental or non-profit entity for the purpose of maintaining the areas in their natural or landscaped condition. … The use of nonfunctional turfgrass and nonfunctional artificial turfgrass in common landscape areas is prohibited.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.08.02.04.B.6 and C.2, Identification of Landscape Areas (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). C applies to single-family detached, duplex, townhome and multiplex development.

fact: Loveland's development code defines a structure to include playground equipment, fences and swimming pools, while leaving out grade changes, hardscapes and play court surfaces.
quote: Structure means anything other than a building that is constructed, erected, or installed, the use of which requires more or less permanent location on the ground, and the form of which extends above or below ground, including, but not limited to fences, walls, gazebos, playground equipment, satellite dishes or antennae, communications towers, swimming pools, and flag poles. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this definition, the word “structure” does not include grade changes ( e.g. , berms), streets, sidewalks, parking lots or spaces, hardscapes, play court surfaces, irrigation ditches, or reservoirs.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Structure" (Ord. 6326, effective Sept. 3, 2019)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's development code names dog runs and animal pens, along with detached garages, carports and sheds, as examples of accessory structures on a residential lot.
quote: Examples of accessory structures include, but are not limited to: detached garages, carports, sheds, dog runs, and animal pens that are accessory to residential buildings, storage buildings that are accessory to lumberyards, and restroom facilities that are accessory to parks.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Accessory Structure" (as amended by Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland keeps an accessory structure at least as far back from the front lot line as the house and five feet from interior side and alley lot lines, and at the interior rear five feet or one foot for every four feet of height, whichever is greater.
quote: Setbacks. Accessory Structures shall be set back from the applicable lot lines as follows: … Front: Equal to or greater than the actual front setback for the principal dwelling or building with which it is associated; … Interior Side: Five feet. … Interior Rear: Five feet or one foot for every four feet of building height, whichever is greater. … Alley: Five feet.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.04.07.02.B, Accessory Structures (effective Jan. 20, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). Sec. 18.04.07.02.D.2 exempts temporary accessory structures under 36 inches tall from these setbacks.

fact: Loveland exempts temporary accessory structures under 36 inches tall from accessory setbacks and leaves any setback reduction for other temporary structures to the Director.
quote: Structures less than 36 inches in height are not subject to the setback requirements listed in Section 18.04.07.01.B Setbacks. … The Director may allow a reduction in setbacks for temporary accessory structures if determined that such reduction will not have detrimental impacts on surrounding property and all other provisions in this Section have been met.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.04.07.02.D and Division 18.19.03, "Temporary Accessory Structure"
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for Sec. 18.04.07.02.D (Ord. 6805, effective 2026-01-20). D.2 cites 18.04.07.01.B as written in the code (the setbacks sit in 18.04.07.02.B). The definition of a temporary accessory structure is its own record (loveland-co.udc-temporary-accessory-def, secid 4235).

fact: Loveland defines a temporary accessory structure as one that exists on an impermanent basis, is not on a permanent foundation and does not need a building permit.
quote: Temporary Accessory Structure means a structure that exists on an impermanent basis, is not placed on a permanent foundation, and does not require a building permit.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Temporary Accessory Structure" (Ord. 6446, effective Dec. 29, 2020)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view, secid 4235, on 2026-09-25.

fact: Loveland requires residential subdivisions of 50 or more homes to set aside outdoor recreation area at one acre for every 100 homes, which may include playgrounds with tot lots or dog parks, at least 50 feet across and maintained by a property owners' association.
quote: Subdivisions that are created for single family detached dwellings, duplexes, or multiplexes shall include outdoor areas that are designed for recreational activities … Recreation areas may include playgrounds with tot lots, plazas, gathering areas with seating and wildlife viewing, community gardens, dog parks, or active hard surface courts. … Outdoor recreation areas are required at a rate of one acre for every 100 dwelling units for residential subdivisions containing 50 or more residential dwelling units. … The minimum dimension of an outdoor recreation area shall be 50 feet. Small, odd, “left‐over” open space areas, areas within street bufferyards, detention pond two-year storm inundation areas, and areas isolated in corners of the development shall not be included in outdoor recreation areas. … Outdoor recreation areas shall be maintained by a property owners’ association
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.06.03.01, Outdoor Recreation Areas (effective Nov. 20, 2018)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). Applies to residential subdivisions that are not complete neighborhoods (those follow Division 18.06.04).

fact: Loveland requires general multifamily developments of more than 20 units to provide on-site amenities, and its list names play fields, dog parks where pets are allowed, play courts and tot lots.
quote: On-Site Amenities. General multifamily developments that include more than 20 dwelling units shall provide on-site amenities as set forth in this subsection. … Outdoor Passive amenities include paths; picnic areas; play fields and; dog parks (if pets are allowed), and other facilities with a comparable amenity value. Outdoor Active Level One amenities include play courts and tot lots with appropriate equipment, lighting, and seating for adults, and other facilities with a comparable amenity value.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.06.07.03, General Multifamily
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland allows state-licensed family child care homes, large child care homes included, in any dwelling unit without a city permit, and keeps two large child care homes from sitting immediately next to each other on the same street segment.
quote: The following child care uses are allowed without a permit in all dwelling units, provided that all licenses (if any) that are required by state law (see 12 CCR 2509-8) are obtained prior to establishment of the use, and thereafter maintained: … Large Child Care Homes. In addition to any state regulatory requirements, large child care homes, … shall be spaced from each other so that that there are not two or more such facilities located immediately adjacent and fronting on the same street segment.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.02.06.03, Home Child Care (Ord. 6636, effective Sept. 19, 2023; 12 CCR 2509-8)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland counts a project as redevelopment when more than 75 percent of the floor area on site is demolished and rebuilt and floor area grows at least 50 percent, or when new building permits exceed twice the appraised value of the land and improvements, a test the city says differs from the state law's.
quote: The City of Loveland defines redevelopment as renovation, modification, or reconstruction of a subject property in which: More than 75 percent of the floor area of buildings on site are demolished and reconstructed; and a cumulative increase in the gross floor area of a building or use by at least 50 percent from the effective date of the UDC; or the value of new building permits exceeds two times the appraised value of the existing land and improvements. This definition differs from the Senate Bill’s definition.
source_label: City of Loveland, "Landscape Changes Impacting Developers" project page (Ordinance 6819)
notes: The FAQ adds that the city was developing guidance on how SB 24-005 applies to redevelopment applications and points to UDC 18.19.03.

fact: Loveland says a site-specific development plan is judged under the rules in effect when its complete application was submitted, and that applications submitted after the 2026 code update must meet the new landscape standards.
quote: An application for approval of a site-specific development plan, as well as the approval, conditional approval, or denial of approval of such plan, are governed by the laws and regulations in effect at the time the complete application is submitted. However, all applications submitted after the implementation of the updated UDC must fully comply with the new standards.
source_label: City of Loveland, Landscape Changes FAQ (Let's Talk Loveland)
notes: The update took effect March 17, 2026 (loveland-ord-6819-sb24-005).

fact: The March 3, 2026 council memo for Ordinance 6819’s second reading, summing up the January 20, 2026 first-reading discussion, says artificial turf plans in wildland-urban interface areas will require a Loveland Fire Rescue Authority assessment, and that staff stressed the code gives the Development Services Director flexibility for hardship.
quote: Fire safety concerns in wildland-urban interface (WUI) areas will require assessments by the Loveland Fire Rescue Authority, particularly for any artificial turf plans and landscaping that is fire-resistant. Staff emphasized that the code changes provide the Development Services Director with flexibility to address situations that may involve hardship or circumstances not contemplated by the landscape provisions.
source_label: City of Loveland, City Council agenda item: Ordinance No. 6819, second reading, March 3, 2026 (summary of the January 20, 2026 first reading)
notes: Council memo (agenda item for second reading, March 3, 2026), in its summary of the January 20, 2026 first reading (vote 9-0); not code text. UDC 18.08.02.09 sends WUI Overlay Zone landscaping to Appendix O of the adopted Fire Code.

fact: Loveland's animal code makes owners remove their animal's feces immediately, on private property as well as streets, sidewalks and parks.
quote: It shall be unlawful for the owner or keeper of any animal to fail to remove any feces deposited by such animal on streets, sidewalks, parks and recreation areas, and private property, or in any water immediately after the animal has deposited the fecal matter.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Sec. 6.20.050, Animal waste removal (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser.

fact: Loveland's animal code counts an animal that creates offensive odors materially interfering with a neighbor's lawful use of their home as a public nuisance, and holds the owner strictly liable.
quote: For the purposes of this section, a public nuisance includes an animal which is a safety or health hazard, injures a person or another animal in any manner, damages or destroys public property or the property of another, or creates offensive odors which materially interfere with or disrupt another person in the conduct of lawful activities at such person's home. … it being the intent of this section to impose strict liability upon the animal owner or keeper for the actions, conduct and condition of such animal.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Sec. 6.20.040, Public nuisance (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser.

fact: Loveland's code bars loud and persistent barking but lets an owner be charged only after someone in the household received a written warning from a police or animal control officer within the preceding 12 months.
quote: No owner, keeper or person in charge of an animal shall fail to prevent it from disturbing the peace and quiet of any other person by loud and persistent barking, baying, howling, yipping, crying, yelping, whining, or making any other noise in an excessive, continuous or untimely fashion, whether the animal is on or off the owner's premises. … No owner or keeper of an animal which is alleged to have disturbed the peace and quiet of another person shall be charged with a violation of Subsection A of this section unless the owner or keeper or a member of said person's household has received a written warning from a police officer or an animal control officer within the preceding 12 months.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Sec. 6.20.020, Disturbance of peace and quiet (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser.

fact: Loveland sets no fixed number of household pets: its code allows as many as a home can keep healthy without a health or safety hazard or a nuisance to the neighbors.
quote: No person shall keep, house or maintain in or upon the premises of any residential dwelling unit more pet animals than can be properly maintained in a healthy condition without presenting a health or safety hazard to the owner or keeper, to the pets, or to any others or more pet animals than can be properly maintained without constituting a nuisance to the occupants of neighboring properties.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Sec. 6.28.010, Limitations on the number of household pets (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser.

fact: Loveland requires a city license for each dog or cat within 14 days of getting it, renewed every year.
quote: The owner or keeper of any dog, cat, pot-bellied pig or dwarf goat kept within the city shall secure from the city, within 14 days of acquiring possession of said dog, cat, pot-bellied pig or dwarf goat, a license to keep the animal, which shall at all times be kept current by the owner or keeper. … The applicant shall apply for a renewal license each year.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Secs. 6.08.010 and 6.08.020, License required; application and term (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser. Defenses in 6.08.010.A: the owner has lived in the city under 30 days, or the animal is four months old or younger.

fact: Loveland's code requires a fence used to hold an animal to be built to hold it and kept in good repair, keeps dogs leashed off their owner's premises except in fenced off-leash parks, and bars letting them run at large in apartment and condominium common areas or subdivision open space.
quote: Any animal off its owner's or keeper's premises shall be on a leash or tether controlled by its owner or keeper, except where such animal and its owner or keeper are located within a fenced park specifically designated by a public authority for off-leash or untethered dogs. … No animal owner, or any person who harbors an animal shall fail to prevent the animal from running at large in the yard of any multiple occupancy building which is occupied by other persons; or in the common areas of mobile home complexes, apartments, or condominium developments; or in open space areas of subdivisions; or in public parks, trails or fairgrounds, unless permission is posted by public authorities allowing animals at large. … It shall be unlawful for any keeper or owner who uses a fence to enclose an animal to fail to ensure that the fence is properly and adequately constructed for the purpose of securing the animal within the fenced enclosure and that the fence is kept in good repair to so secure the animal.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Sec. 6.20.010, Animal at large (codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025)
notes: Read through api.municode.com CodesContent (product 15738, job 488583, Supplement 13, codified through Ord. No. 6804, Dec. 16, 2025); library.municode.com renders the same text in a browser.

fact: Loveland's two city dog parks, at Fairgrounds Park and Mehaffey Park, are fenced off-leash areas with a separate enclosure for small or shy dogs, surfaced with material like the Big Thompson River corridor's at Fairgrounds and with crushed fines at Mehaffey to cut down on weed control.
quote: The surface material at the Fairgrounds Park dog park is similar to what would be expected along the Big Thompson River corridor. … The surface material at the Mehaffey Park dog park is a crushed fine type surface to help reduce the need for weed control measures. … Both dog parks are compromised of fenced-in areas which provide dogs and their owners off-leash play and training areas. … Within the dog parks, a separate, fully enclosed section has been designated for the use of small or shy dogs.
source_label: City of Loveland Parks & Recreation, Dog Parks page (Wayback Machine capture, Feb. 17, 2026)
notes: Read from the Wayback Machine capture 20260217034258 (web.archive.org/web/20260217034258/https://www.lovgov.org/services/parks-recreation/parks-facilities/dog-parks); the live page returns HTTP 403 to curl, WebFetch and a headless browser on 2026-09-25, so the capture is the copy read.

quote: Dogs must be vaccinated, licensed and wear the appropriate tags. … You're responsible for any holes or damage created by your dog. … Pets are NOT allowed: in environmentally sensitive areas including Prairie Ridge Natural Area and Morey Wildlife Reserve (in accordance with the conservation easement); inside the Centennial Park Baseball Complex ; on inline hockey rinks, skate park areas, spray parks, basketball and volleyball courts; on the Championship Field at Loveland Sports Park ; or within 100 feet of any other athletic courts or fields while practices or games are being played
source_label: City of Loveland Parks & Recreation, Rules & Regulations page (Wayback Machine capture, April 11, 2026)

fact: After an unusually dry winter, Golf Loveland made every round at its city courses walking-only from February 20, 2026, to keep fragile turf from breaking down further.
quote: Due to extreme conditions created by an unusually dry winter, all golf rounds will be walking only beginning Friday, February 20, 2026. … Limiting cart traffic now helps prevent further degradation of the fragile turf conditions so that, when possible and conditions allow, we can restore the course more quickly and maintain the quality of play we all value.
source_label: Golf Loveland (City of Loveland), Cart Restrictions / dry conditions page (Wayback Machine capture, March 5, 2026)
notes: Read from the Wayback Machine capture 20260305082539 (web.archive.org/web/20260305082539/https://www.golfloveland.com/book-tee-time/dry-conditions); the live page returns HTTP 403 to curl, WebFetch and a headless browser on 2026-09-25, so the capture is the copy read. The Reporter-Herald (Feb. 17, 2026) reported the same suspension at all three municipal courses.

fact: Loveland's golf course superintendent said in February 2026 that if water ran short the greens would be protected first, and that in past dry years the city courses had received as little as 50% of their water shares.
quote: In past dry years, the courses have received as little as 50% of their water shares, Kling said. … Kling said that if water supplies are limited, protecting greens — “where the money’s at,” as he put it — would take priority, potentially leaving some fairway areas to struggle.
source_label: Loveland Reporter-Herald, Feb. 17, 2026: Loveland golf courses suspend carts
notes: News report quoting Course Superintendent Dennis Kling; carts were suspended at all three municipal courses from Friday, Feb. 20, 2026.

fact: Golf Loveland lifted its 2026 cart restrictions on May 18 but kept carts on the path on par-3 holes at Mariana Butte and The Olde Course.

quote: The Mini-Course has 9 holes, each with their own dedicated tee box and green. Average amount of time it takes to play all 9 holes is approximately 45 minutes. … You’ve practiced on the Mini-Course with S.N.A.G® clubs
source_label: Golf Loveland, Cattail Creek Mini-Course (S.N.A.G.) page, Wayback Machine capture of Aug. 10, 2025
notes: Read from the Wayback Machine capture 20250810003457; the live golfloveland.com pages return HTTP 403. The page is about S.N.A.G. (starter golf) play, not a putting course.

fact: The Reserve at Mariana Butte, a 91-lot single-family HOA formed in 1994 as the city built its Mariana Butte golf course, is one of several HOAs around the course.
quote: The Reserve at Mariana Butte Homeowners’ Association (HOA) formed in 1994 as the City of Loveland expanded to the west and built the city-owned Mariana Butte golf course. The HOA represents 91 member lots. All are single family homes. The Reserve is one of several HOAs in the area surrounding the golf course.
source_label: The Reserve at Mariana Butte HOA, About page

fact: The Reserve at Mariana Butte’s landscape design guidelines, updated February 7, 2024, limit artificial turf to back yards and require any customized landscape plan anywhere on a lot to be reviewed and approved by the HOA’s Architectural Review Committee before the work.
quote: The HOA Architectural Review Committee (ARC) should be included in any consideration for changes to the exterior appearance of your home or landscaping as outlined in our Conditions, Covenants & Restrictions documents. … Use of artificial or non-vegetative turf is limited to back yards. … Any customized plan for anywhere on your property must be reviewed and approved by the ARC committee prior to any landscape modification of the homeowners’ lot.
source_label: The Reserve at Mariana Butte HOA Landscape Design Guidelines, updated Feb. 7, 2024

fact: Kinston at Centerra's November 2025 home builder design guidelines allow lawn only where it serves a usable space such as a patio extension, a play area or an outdoor room, in areas of at least 100 contiguous square feet and 8 feet wide, capped at 25% of a lot's landscaped area, or 40% with an alternative grass such as buffalo grass, without Design Review Board approval.
quote: Lawn. Lawn shall be limited to areas with a minimum of 100 contiguous square feet and a minimum width of 8’. Lawn shall be utilized only where associated with usable spaces such as an extension of a patio, a play area, or as an outdoor room. Lawn shall not exceed 25% of Total Landscaped Area, or 40% if an alternative lawn grass (such as Buffalo grass) is used in lieu of a traditional fescue blend, without DRB approval.
source_label: Kinston at Centerra, Home Builder Design Guidelines, November 2025 (McWhinney), Landscape section
notes: A search of the full document (8,000+ lines of text) found no mention of artificial or synthetic turf; the lawn rules speak to living lawn.

fact: Thompson School District, Loveland's school district, closes its fields to community groups January through March to protect spring field conditions and posts separate rules for its synthetic turf field.
quote: District fields will be closed to community groups January through March to maintain optimal spring field conditions. … Turf Field Rules and Regulations … Reglas y Regulaciones del Campo de Césped Sintético
source_label: Thompson School District, Facility Use page
notes: The page also notes special rental costs for Ray Patterson field; which field the turf rules cover is not stated on the page.

fact: Loveland's development code defines a parkway as the landscaped strip between the sidewalk and the curb, which earlier versions of the code called a street tree lawn.
quote: Parkway means a strip of landscaped area between the sidewalk and curb. Parkways were referred to as street tree lawns in previous versions of the Unified Development Code.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Parkway" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's development code defines common interest community property as property an owners' association owns and maintains, such as entryways, parks and other common amenities.
quote: Common Interest Community Property means property within a common interest community that is owned and maintained by an owners' association, such as entryways, parks, and other common amenities or elements.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Common Interest Community Property" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's development code defines a common green as an accessible area of a development, usually owned in common, for passive or recreational activities, and counts turfgrass on it as functional when it supports those activities.
quote: Common Green means an accessible area of land within a development, typically under common interest community ownership, designated for both passive and/or recreational activities. Turfgrass within common greens is considered functional when it supports these recreational activities.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Common Green" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's development code counts living turfgrass as functional in recreational or regularly used civic and community spaces, naming cemeteries, playgrounds, sports fields, picnic grounds, amphitheaters, high-use parts of parks such as team warm-up areas, and golf playing areas.
quote: Functional Turfgrass means turfgrass located in a recreational use area or other space that is regularly used for civic, community, or recreational purposes, which may include cemeteries; playgrounds; sports fields; picnic grounds; amphitheaters; ancillary high use portions of parks (e.g., sports team warm up areas); and the playing areas of a golf course or driving range.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Functional Turfgrass" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's code counts living turf in rights-of-way, parking lots, medians and transportation corridors as nonfunctional, but leaves out turfgrass that is part of a permit-required water quality treatment solution, as long as it is not irrigated and no herbicides are applied.
quote: Nonfunctional Turfgrass means turfgrass that is not serving a functional purpose. It includes turf located in street rights-of-way, parking lots, medians, or transportation corridors. It excludes turfgrass that is part of a water quality treatment solution required for compliance with federal, state, or local water quality permitting requirements, provided that the turfgrass is not irrigated and no herbicides are applied.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Division 18.19.03, "Nonfunctional Turfgrass" (Ord. 6819, effective March 17, 2026)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17). The artificial-turf definition (secid 5935) carries no such water-quality exclusion.

fact: Loveland's parking lot landscaping standards reach surface lots of more than 15 spaces in most zones (30 in a complete neighborhood's activity center, 75 downtown) and require at least 75 percent of the landscaped area inside the lot to be covered with established living materials within three years, with separators in stand-alone lots of more than 200 spaces.
quote: This section applies to any surface parking lot that contains more than: a. 75 parking spaces in the DT zone; b. 30 parking spaces in the neighborhood activity center of a complete neighborhood; or c. 15 parking spaces in all other zones or areas. … at least 75 percent of landscaped areas within a parking lot shall be covered with established living materials within three years of installation. … Parking lot islands and landscaped areas shall be at least six inches above the surface of the parking lot and protected with concrete curbing, except where designed specifically for the absorption of stormwater. … a large surface parking lot is a stand-alone surface parking lot that contains more than 200 parking spaces.
source_label: Loveland Municipal Code Title 18 (Unified Development Code), Sec. 18.08.04.03, Parking Lots (as amended by Ord. 6819)
notes: Read from encodePlus doc-view for this section (the codified Title 18, including Ord. 6819 amendments effective 2026-03-17).

fact: Loveland's FAQ on the 2026 landscape changes says the state law requires nonfunctional turf to be removed for projects that need a building permit or any site-specific development plan, and that because the city's and the state's definitions of redevelopment differ, the city is developing more specific guidance for redevelopment applications.
quote: SB 24-005 requires removal of non-functional turf for projects that require a Building Permit or any site-specific development plan. … Because these definitions of “redevelopment” vary, the City of Loveland is developing more specific guidance on how SB 24-005 regulations apply to redevelopment applications through the UDC update process.
source_label: City of Loveland, Landscape Changes FAQ (Let's Talk Loveland)
notes: The FAQ page reads as written before the UDC update took effect on 2026-03-17; recheck for the promised redevelopment guidance.

fact: Loveland's project page on the 2026 landscape changes says the state turf law mostly restricts cool-season, high-water grasses such as Kentucky bluegrass and fescues, not native or climate-adapted grasses, and names buffalo grass and blue grama as climate-adapted examples.
quote: Generally, turf restricted under SB 24-005 will be cool-season varieties with high water demand, such as Kentucky bluegrass or fescues. Native or climate-adapted turfgrasses are not restricted under SB 24-005. … Climate-Adapted Grasses - Naturally suited grasses that thrive in specific climate conditions, requiring less maintenance and resources. Examples include Buffalo Grass, Blue Grama Grass, and Bermuda Grass, which are adapted to hot and dry climates.
source_label: City of Loveland, "Landscape Changes Impacting Developers" project page (Ordinance 6819)
notes: The page notes that definitions in the UDC update may differ from these project definitions.

fact: Thompson School District's rules for its synthetic turf field bar food and drinks other than water, gum, candy, nuts and sunflower seeds, dogs, metal cleats and high heels, stakes and field marking or paint, and snow removal the district has not authorized.
quote: The following are PROHIBITED on synthetic turf field areas: Food or drinks (except water) Chewing gum, candy, nuts or sunflower seeds Dogs or other animals … Metal cleats or high heeled shoes (cleats must be rubber or plastic) Stakes, posts, poles or markers of any kind Marking, painting or taping the field Unauthorized snow removal
source_label: Thompson School District, Turf Field Rules & Regulations (PDF linked from the district's Facility Use page)
notes: The link redirects to a one-page PDF on resources.finalsite.net (TSDTurfFieldRulesRegulations.pdf). Which district field it governs is not named.
